title: Implement Self-Service Analytics for Operational and Commercial Teams
narrative: Analytical reporting at FEDC is currently centralised in a data team that builds and maintains reports for operational and commercial stakeholders. Teams submit report requests, which are typically fulfilled within two weeks. This bottleneck means that business questions are answered slowly, and teams use workarounds — manual spreadsheet analysis, shadow data stores — that create data quality and governance risks. We propose implementing a self-service analytics capability that enables operational and commercial teams to query and visualise authorised data without dependency on the central data team. The capability will be built on the existing data warehouse, extended with a semantic layer that exposes business-friendly metrics. Role-based access will ensure teams can only access data appropriate to their function. Training and enablement will be provided to 150 analysts in the first year.

requirements.title: Self-service query capability
requirements.description: Business analysts must be able to build and run reports against authorised data domains without writing SQL or requiring data team assistance for standard query patterns.

requirements.title: Semantic layer
requirements.description: All self-service metrics must be defined in a semantic layer that translates business terminology to underlying data structures, ensuring consistent metric definitions across teams.

requirements.title: Query performance
requirements.description: Self-service queries against datasets of up to 100 million rows must complete within 30 seconds for 95% of executed queries.

recommendations.recommendation: **'Semantic layer'** is technical jargon unfamiliar to business stakeholders. Replace with plain language: *'A business-friendly metrics layer that translates technical database names into familiar business terms (e.g., "monthly revenue", "customer count").'* This clarifies the business value without requiring technical expertise to understand.

The phrase **'standard query patterns'** in the first requirement is undefined. Clarify: Do you mean predefined report templates? Drag-and-drop filters? A specific set of aggregation types (e.g., filtered summaries over 3 dimensions)? Downstream design work needs precision here to scope the platform correctly.

The narrative emphasises **role-based access** as a governance control, but no requirement explicitly captures this. Add a Non-Functional requirement: 'Access to data must be restricted by role based on business function, and all access attempts must be logged for audit purposes.' This makes governance intent measurable.

The narrative and requirements are well-structured, clear on the business problem and measurable outcomes. They are ready for downstream architecture analysis. Consider clarifying scope: Does role-based access prevent access to *metrics* (which metrics a role can query) or to *data rows* (filters on results), or both? This distinction drives the semantic layer design.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision implements self-service analytics to address a centralised data team bottleneck. This capability directly realises **Data Architecture Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle DAT-PRN-003 (Quality is a producer responsibility) and DAT-PRN-002 (Define once, use everywhere), by requiring a business-friendly semantic layer and ensuring consistent metric definitions across teams.
impact-assessment.impact: Self-service analytics cannot succeed without strong governance of metric definitions and data quality. The proposed semantic layer is a logical control that must be referenced in `DAT-PRN` to enforce consistency. Without explicit principles binding the semantic layer to canonical definitions, teams risk re-creating shadow metrics that undermine the single-source-of-truth intent.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Add a principle to DAT-PRN** that captures the governance model for the semantic layer: e.g., 'All self-service metrics must be defined in a semantic layer that translates to canonical data concepts; metrics not in the semantic layer cannot be queried by business users.' This ensures downstream teams building the self-service platform know their control boundary.
impact-assessment.rationale: Semantic layers are infrastructure; governance principles tell the infrastructure team what rules it must enforce. DAT-PRN is the contract between the architecture and the platform. Without an explicit principle, the semantic layer becomes a technical implementation detail rather than a governed asset, increasing risk of metric proliferation.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision implements a new **self-service analytics capability** using role-based access control (RBAC) to constrain data visibility by business function. This is a new data access pattern not currently represented in **Data Architecture Guardrails** (`DAT-GRD`), which defines non-negotiable enforcement rules for the Data domain.
impact-assessment.impact: Role-based access enforcement at the semantic layer is a guardrail — a mandatory control that prevents unauthorised data visibility. If DAT-GRD does not explicitly require RBAC enforcement and audit logging for self-service queries, downstream teams may implement self-service without the governance safeguards needed to satisfy compliance and risk requirements.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Add a guardrail to DAT-GRD** that mandates: (1) All self-service query access is role-based and linked to business function; (2) Denied or anomalous access attempts are logged; (3) Role-to-data mappings are reviewed quarterly. This makes the control non-negotiable for the platform team.
impact-assessment.rationale: Self-service democratises access; GDPR, data privacy regulations, and internal risk policy require that scale-up in access be matched by scale-up in enforcement visibility. A guardrail signals to the platform team that access control is not optional and must be auditable.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision targets **operational and commercial teams** (approximately 150 analysts) as end-users. No explicit requirement captures enablement or skills, yet the decision narrative emphasises 'training and enablement' as a first-year deliverable. This cross-cuts from Data architecture into **Business Capabilities** — specifically, **Manage Customer Insight** (`CAP-001-03`) and **Manage Finance** (`CAP-009-01`), both of which will consume self-service analytics.
impact-assessment.impact: If the self-service analytics platform is built without coordinating with the skill and organisational readiness of the consuming teams, uptake will be slow. The 150 analysts are internal users of the new capability — they must be trained and their team structures may need to evolve to absorb self-service workflows. This is architectural scope that reaches beyond the Data domain into operating model and business capability delivery.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Review and update BUS-CAP** to reflect the new data analytics workload and skill requirements in the relevant business capabilities — notably `CAP-001-03` (Manage Customer Insight) and `CAP-009-01` (Manage Finance). Consider whether the architecture should reference an enablement artefact (e.g. a new role taxonomy or skill matrix) that links the platform capability to the people and teams that operate it. Current artefact types do not capture enablement; if needed, flag as a future artefact-type addition.
impact-assessment.rationale: Business capabilities describe *what the business does*, including how it deploys its people. Self-service analytics redistributes capability ownership away from the central data team to business teams. The BUS-CAP model should reflect that shift, making it visible in executive reviews that the organisation must actively build new skills in 150 users.

impact-assessment.finding: The self-service platform will operate alongside the existing data warehouse and will require **Application Domains & Platforms** (`APP-DAP`) updates. The decision scope statement names `DAT-PRN`, but the semantic layer and query interface are applications — they sit in **APP-DOM-DATA** (Data & Analytics domain) under **PLAT-BI** (BI & Analytics platform, lifecycle: adopt) and **PLAT-DATA-LAKEHOUSE** (Data Lakehouse, lifecycle: adopt).
impact-assessment.impact: If APP-DAP is not updated to explicitly capture the semantic layer as a platform component or service, the Application architecture will not reflect the new logical separation between raw data (lakehouse) and business-friendly query surface (semantic layer). This can lead to downstream platform teams treating the semantic layer as configuration rather than as a distinct architectural element with its own governance and evolution path.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Add or update APP-DAP** to capture the semantic layer as either: (1) a new platform under APP-DOM-DATA (e.g., `PLAT-SEMANTIC-LAYER`), or (2) an explicit sub-component or service within `PLAT-BI` or `PLAT-DATA-LAKEHOUSE`. Document its type (system-of-insight or system-of-record) and lifecycle intent (adopt). Ensure **Application Architecture Principles** (`APP-PRN`) includes guidance on how semantic layers relate to the broader Application landscape (e.g., do they expose stable APIs? are they versioned?).
impact-assessment.rationale: Application architecture tracks the platforms that realise data capabilities. The semantic layer is not a data artefact — it is an application that sits between the user and the warehouse. Treating it explicitly in APP-DAP makes it visible for capacity planning, dependency management, and vendor/platform evolution decisions.

impact-assessment.finding: The decision narrative states that self-service will address 'standard query patterns' but does not define what these are. **Data Architecture Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) and **Data Architecture Strategy** (`DAT-STR`) together set the foundation for what the data platform supports; without alignment on 'standard' patterns, the semantic layer risks becoming a dumping ground for every ad-hoc query shape that consuming teams demand, undermining the governance intent of the semantic layer.
impact-assessment.impact: Scope creep on the semantic layer is common in self-service analytics projects. Without principle-driven constraints, the platform team will face pressure to expose new metrics and query patterns for every business team request, leading to a fragmented, unsustainable semantic layer and delaying or degrading the 30-second query performance target for large datasets.
impact-assessment.recommendation: **Clarify and document 'standard query patterns' as part of the ADR resolution**: document in `DAT-PRN` what query shapes the semantic layer will support (e.g., 'filtered aggregations over up to 3 dimensions') and what it will not (e.g., 'freeform exploratory SQL'). This becomes a governance rule that the platform team can enforce. If 'standard patterns' are already defined elsewhere, reference them; if not, define them before platform build begins.
impact-assessment.rationale: Governance is most effective when rules are precise and enforceable. Semantic layers without constraints become maintenance nightmares. A principle that defines the boundary of 'standard' is a design input to the platform team and a deflection mechanism for out-of-scope requests.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 directly advances **Data Strategy** (`DAT-STR`) statement *'Default to self-service; specialist data teams support domains, not gate them'* (DAT-STR-003). The self-service analytics capability shifts the operating model from ticket-based report delivery (centralised data team) to autonomous querying by business analysts, eliminating the bottleneck identified in the decision narrative.
strategy-alignment.impact: This decision realises the medium-term target outcome of DAT-STR-003 ('80% of analytics use cases satisfied without bespoke pipeline work'). By enabling operational and commercial teams to build and run reports without data team assistance, the decision frees specialist capacity to focus on platform improvements and data governance — a direct strategic gain.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Ensure the implementation plan explicitly measures progress toward the DAT-STR-003 target. Define metrics: e.g., percentage of analytics queries served by self-service vs. bespoke work, and the reallocation of data team capacity to platform and governance work. Document these in the project charter.
strategy-alignment.rationale: DAT-STR-003 is a strategic shift from request-driven to platform-driven delivery. Explicit metrics tie the decision outcome to the strategic objective and help track whether the implementation is achieving the intended operating-model change.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 advances **Data Strategy** statement *'Federate data ownership to domain teams; centralise only standards and platform'* (DAT-STR-002). The semantic layer acts as a centralised standard (business-friendly metrics defined once) while empowering domain teams (operational and commercial analysts) to consume and query those metrics autonomously, implementing the federated-ownership model.
strategy-alignment.impact: The decision distributes analytics capability away from the central data team, aligning with the medium-term target of DAT-STR-002 ('Every data product has a named domain owner; a single self-service platform with shared standards by 2026'). This reduces bottleneck risk and improves time-to-insight for consuming teams.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Define and document the data ownership boundaries: which metrics belong to which domain, and who (in each domain) is accountable for metric definition and quality. Link this explicitly to the semantic layer design — ensure the semantic layer's structure reflects domain ownership, not a flat, undifferentiated metric repository.
strategy-alignment.rationale: Federated ownership only works if domains are clearly delineated. The semantic layer is the governance mechanism; its structure and metadata must encode ownership, so consuming teams know whom to contact for metric changes.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 strongly advances **Business Strategy** statement *'Decide with data — every material business decision must cite the evidence that supports it'* (BUS-STR-003). The self-service analytics capability directly realises the target outcome of BUS-STR-003 ('Self-serve analytics available to every team'), by enabling 150 analysts in operational and commercial functions to query and visualise authorised data independently.
strategy-alignment.impact: This decision removes a structural barrier to evidence-driven decision-making: slow analytics turnaround. By reducing the time from question to insight (from two weeks to real-time query execution), the decision increases the likelihood that teams will cite data in decisions, advancing the strategic objective of BUS-STR-003.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Include in the project communications an emphasis on *decision-making speed* as the business benefit. When training the 150 analysts, highlight that self-service enables faster evidence gathering and thus faster, better decisions. Track adoption through decision logs and team surveys to measure whether the capability is being used as intended.
strategy-alignment.rationale: BUS-STR-003 is not just about analytics access; it is about behaviour change — making data-driven decision-making the norm. The self-service platform is enabling infrastructure; adoption and behaviour change are the strategic outcomes. Explicit focus on decision-making speed reinforces the strategic intent.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 advances **Business Strategy** statement *'Build digital-by-default operations — paper, manual handovers, and bespoke spreadsheets are exceptions, not the norm'* (BUS-STR-005). The decision narrative explicitly identifies shadow data stores and manual spreadsheet analysis as current workarounds; the self-service analytics capability replaces these with a governed, digital analytics platform.
strategy-alignment.impact: This decision directly addresses the operational inefficiency identified in BUS-STR-005. By moving analytical work from spreadsheets to a managed platform, the decision contributes to the target outcome ('Top 20 business processes fully digital end-to-end by 2026') and reduces data quality and governance risks created by shadow systems.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: As part of project scope, explicitly plan the migration of current spreadsheet-based reports into the self-service semantic layer. Document which spreadsheets are in scope and estimate the effort to formalise their metrics. This makes the shift from manual to digital visible and measurable.
strategy-alignment.rationale: Digital-by-default is achieved through deliberate migration, not by waiting for natural adoption. Explicit scope and tracking ensure that the self-service platform displaces shadow systems rather than existing alongside them.

strategy-alignment.finding: ADR-013 does not explicitly address **Data Strategy** principle *'Privacy and consent are designed in, not bolted on'* (DAT-STR-004). The decision narrative mentions role-based access control but does not emphasise privacy design (e.g., personal data minimisation, consent traceability, or privacy-aware semantic layer design).
strategy-alignment.impact: Self-service analytics at scale expands data access to 150 new users. Without explicit privacy design, the platform risks creating compliance gaps: unauthorised exposure of personal data, inadequate consent records, or inability to trace which users accessed what data. This is a material gap given FEDC's regulatory environment.
strategy-alignment.recommendation: Add a requirement to the decision: 'The semantic layer must implement privacy-by-design principles, including (1) personal data classification in the semantic model; (2) consent-linked data masking or filtering; (3) audit logging of all access to personal data.' Reference DAT-STR-004 explicitly in the design brief to signal that privacy is non-negotiable, not an afterthought.
strategy-alignment.rationale: DAT-STR-004 is short-term (horizon: short-term), making it a near-term priority. Self-service analytics must be designed with privacy from the start, not retrofitted later. Explicit requirement language ensures the platform team knows this is a strategic design input, not a compliance checklist item.

referential-integrity.finding: **Data Architecture Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle references are sound. DAT-PRN-003 and DAT-PRN-002 both exist and are correctly identified in the impact assessment. All principle IDs resolve to defined entities.
referential-integrity.impact: The decision's citation of existing principles ensures architecture traceability and evidence-based recommendations.
referential-integrity.recommendation: No action required — all Data Architecture Principles citations resolve correctly.
referential-integrity.rationale: Referential integrity for principles validates that the decision is grounded in established governance, not inventing new rules.

referential-integrity.finding: **Data Architecture Guardrails** (`DAT-GRD`) is referenced in the impact-assessment section with a recommendation to add guardrails for self-service access control, but the current `DAT-GRD` catalogue at `architectures/clients/fedc/1.0.0/domains/data/physical/DAT-GRD.json` contains an empty `guardrails` array. The catalogue structure exists, but no guardrail entities are defined.
referential-integrity.impact: The absence of defined guardrails means the recommended control ('All self-service query access is role-based...') cannot yet be referenced. Until guardrails are added to the `DAT-GRD` catalogue, downstream teams will lack an authoritative source for mandatory Data domain enforcement rules.
referential-integrity.recommendation: As part of ADR-013 resolution, add the recommended guardrails to `DAT-GRD`: (1) self-service query access is role-based and linked to business function; (2) denied or anomalous access attempts are logged; (3) role-to-data mappings are reviewed quarterly. Once added, update the impact-assessment section to reference the new guardrail IDs.
referential-integrity.rationale: Guardrails are enforceable rules, not aspirational statements. Referential integrity requires that every guardrail cited in architecture decisions points to a defined entity in the authoritative catalogue, so platform teams know which rules to implement.

referential-integrity.finding: **Business Capabilities** (`BUS-CAP`) references are sound. Capabilities `CAP-001-03` (Manage Customer Insight) and `CAP-009-01` (Manage Finance) both exist at level 2, with valid parent IDs (`CAP-001` and `CAP-009` respectively). All parent references resolve correctly.
referential-integrity.impact: The decision's identification of consuming business capabilities ensures the self-service analytics capability is explicitly linked to the business functions it enables.
referential-integrity.recommendation: No action required — all Business Capabilities citations resolve correctly.
referential-integrity.rationale: Linking architectural decisions to business capabilities ensures decisions are traceable to business outcomes and prevents orphaned capabilities.

referential-integrity.finding: **Application Domains & Platforms** (`APP-DAP`) references are sound. Domain `APP-DOM-DATA`, platform `PLAT-BI`, and platform `PLAT-DATA-LAKEHOUSE` all exist with correct domain-id references. All platform-to-domain associations are valid.
referential-integrity.impact: The decision's identification of the application platforms enables downstream teams to understand the technology scope and evolution path for self-service analytics.
referential-integrity.recommendation: No action required — all Application Domains & Platforms citations resolve correctly.
referential-integrity.rationale: Platform references ensure decisions connect architectural decisions to the concrete systems that realise them.

referential-integrity.finding: **Integrity summary:** All references to defined entities in `DAT-PRN`, `BUS-CAP`, and `APP-DAP` resolve correctly. The single integrity issue is that `DAT-GRD` (the catalogue where guardrails live) is structurally present but currently empty. The impact-assessment makes a valid recommendation to populate it, which resolves the integrity gap.
referential-integrity.impact: The decision can proceed with the understanding that the recommended guardrails must be added to `DAT-GRD` during resolution in order for platform teams to have an authoritative reference.
referential-integrity.recommendation: Treat the addition of guardrails to `DAT-GRD` as part of the ADR-013 resolution workflow. Once guardrails are added, verify their IDs against the impact-assessment recommendations.
referential-integrity.rationale: Referential integrity is achieved when every reference points to a defined entity and every required entity is defined. This decision's recommendations create the missing entity (guardrails), so integrity will be established during resolution.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Define once, use everywhere'* (DAT-PRN-002) is **adhered to**. The decision explicitly mandates a semantic layer that 'translates business terminology to underlying data structures, ensuring consistent metric definitions across teams.' This centralised, canonical definition is the core mechanism for enforcing DAT-PRN-002.
principles-alignment.impact: Adherence to DAT-PRN-002 is critical to the decision's success. Without a single, authoritative semantic layer, consuming teams will create parallel metric definitions, fragmenting the self-service platform and undermining the governance intent.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Document in the implementation plan how the semantic layer will enforce the 'define once' principle: e.g., metadata governance controls that prevent teams from creating custom metric definitions outside the semantic layer, audit trails for metric changes, and a review process for new metrics.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-002 exists to prevent silent divergence. The self-service analytics capability scales the number of metric consumers from a few (data team) to 150 (operational and commercial analysts). Without strict 'define once' enforcement, the platform will degrade into a fragmented metrics repository.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Quality is a producer responsibility'* (DAT-PRN-003) is **adhered to**. The decision narrative states that 'teams can only access data appropriate to their function' through role-based access, and the semantic layer mediates access to 'authorised data.' This positions the data producer (centralised platform) as responsible for quality and access governance, not the consuming analyst.
principles-alignment.impact: Adherence ensures that data quality expectations are explicitly owned by the platform team, not pushed downstream to consumers. This prevents the common self-service anti-pattern of 'consumers re-cleanse data at query time.'
principles-alignment.recommendation: Include in the semantic layer design a quality attestation model: each metric exposed via the semantic layer must have a defined SLA (e.g., refresh frequency, expected completeness). Document quality issues and escalation paths in the platform runbook.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-003 protects against distributed quality debt. As the platform scales to 150 users, the producer must own quality explicitly, or the platform becomes a distribution mechanism for data-quality problems.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Privacy by design'* (DAT-PRN-004) is **silent — a material gap**. The decision narrative mentions role-based access control but does not address personal-data classification, consent traceability, or privacy-aware semantic layer design. This is a critical silence given the scale (150 new users) and regulatory environment.
principles-alignment.impact: The silence creates a compliance risk. Self-service analytics at scale expands data access without explicit privacy-design controls. Consumers may unknowingly access personal data without knowing consent constraints, and the platform lacks audit trails for personal-data access. This violates the principle's core intent ('privacy from capture, not retrofitted').
principles-alignment.recommendation: Add explicit privacy-design requirements to the decision: (1) personal-data fields are classified in the semantic layer; (2) consent-linked masking or filtering is applied at query time; (3) all access to personal data is audited; (4) the semantic layer design document includes a privacy threat model. Reference DAT-PRN-004 by ID to signal that privacy is non-negotiable.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-004 is short-term strategic priority. Self-service analytics makes privacy-design decisions visible to 150 users; if privacy is not designed in from the start, compliance retrofits will be expensive and incomplete.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Every data domain has an owner'* (DAT-PRN-001) is **silent**. The decision narrative does not identify who owns the semantic layer itself or who is accountable for its metrics, definitions, and lifecycle. While the semantic layer is governance infrastructure (centralised), the principle requires that 'each data domain in DAT-DAC has a single accountable steward.'
principles-alignment.impact: The silence creates ambiguity about accountability. If the semantic layer is viewed as a shared utility with no clear owner, disputes over metric definitions will lack an escalation path and changes will be slow or contested.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Before platform build begins, define the semantic layer ownership model: Is it owned by the central data team, or by a rotating domain steward? Document who is accountable for metric definitions, change review, and SLA compliance. Link this explicitly to the ADR resolution and to the data governance working group.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-001 recognises that unowned data drifts in quality and meaning. A semantic layer is owned data infrastructure; without clear stewardship, it will become unmaintainable or untrustworthy.

principles-alignment.finding: **Data Principles** (`DAT-PRN`) principle *'Open contracts, open standards'* (DAT-PRN-005) is **implicitly adhered to** but not explicitly documented. The decision does not specify the technical format or interface for the semantic layer (e.g., API, SQL interface, JSON Schema), so it is unclear whether the 'open contracts' principle will be satisfied in implementation.
principles-alignment.impact: If the semantic layer implementation uses proprietary or undocumented query formats, downstream consumers (analysts and other applications) will be locked into the platform, reducing reuse and limiting vendor portability.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Document in the design brief that the semantic layer's query interface must be schema-documented and standards-based (e.g., SQL, GraphQL, or REST with OpenAPI). Require the platform team to publish the semantic layer's contract before implementation. This makes DAT-PRN-005 enforceable.
principles-alignment.rationale: DAT-PRN-005 prevents vendor and format lock-in. At self-service scale, many consumers will depend on the semantic layer's interface; locking them into a proprietary format is a long-term operational risk.

principles-alignment.finding: **Business Principles** (`BUS-PRN`) principle *'Process digital by default'* (BUS-PRN-006) is **strongly adhered to**. The decision explicitly addresses shadow spreadsheet analysis and manual workarounds as the current state problem; the self-service analytics capability moves analytical work from spreadsheets and manual processes to a governed digital platform.
principles-alignment.impact: Strong alignment with BUS-PRN-006 increases the likelihood of adoption and operational efficiency. By removing the spreadsheet friction point, the decision removes a barrier to digital-by-default operations.
principles-alignment.recommendation: In project communications and rollout, explicitly link the self-service platform to the BUS-PRN-006 strategic objective. When training the 150 analysts, highlight that self-service replaces manual spreadsheet work with governed, auditable analytics. Track spreadsheet displacement as a success metric.
principles-alignment.rationale: BUS-PRN-006 drives digital excellence. Self-service analytics is a concrete realisation of the principle; making this explicit in communications reinforces the strategic intent.

principles-alignment.finding: **Application Principles** (`APP-PRN`) principle *'Observability is built in, not bolted on'* (APP-PRN-005) is **silent**. The decision does not specify that the self-service platform will include observability (health checks, structured logs, metrics, traces) from day one. This is material because consumption patterns and query performance are critical to the success and operations of the platform.
principles-alignment.impact: Without built-in observability, the operations team will lack visibility into query patterns, performance degradation, and user adoption. Troubleshooting will be slow, and the platform will be difficult to scale as analytics volume grows.
principles-alignment.recommendation: Add a non-functional requirement to the decision: 'The self-service platform must expose health endpoints, structure logs in machine-readable format, emit RED metrics (request rate, error rate, duration) for all queries, and support distributed tracing. Observability must be configured and tested before production launch.'
principles-alignment.rationale: APP-PRN-005 is a non-negotiable quality standard for applications. The semantic layer and query interface are applications; without observability built in from day one, operations teams will be flying blind, increasing the risk of outages and degraded user experience.

challenger-analysis.finding: **Privacy-by-design is not addressed** in the narrative, despite the decision scaling data access from a small data team to 150 operational and commercial analysts. **DAT-PRN-004** ('Privacy by design') is a short-term strategic priority, yet the decision is silent on personal-data classification, consent traceability, and privacy-aware semantic layer design. Self-service analytics dramatically expands the surface area for unintended personal-data exposure.
challenger-analysis.impact: The decision creates **compliance and regulatory risk**. At scale (150 analysts), the probability of accidental personal-data exposure increases materially. Without privacy-design controls (consent-linked masking, audit trails for personal-data access, data classification in the semantic model), the platform becomes a distribution mechanism for uncontrolled personal-data visibility. A single privacy incident — especially involving GDPR or data-protection violations — could trigger audit findings, regulatory penalties, and reputational damage. **Reversal cost is very high**: once data is exposed via the platform, privacy retrofits are expensive and incomplete.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: **Do not proceed to platform build until privacy-design requirements are added to the decision.** Required additions: (1) Personal-data fields must be classified in the semantic layer before deployment; (2) Consent-linked data masking or filtering must be applied at query time; (3) All access to personal data must be audited with full traceability (user, query, timestamp, data accessed); (4) A privacy threat model must be completed and reviewed by Data Security and Legal before launch. These are non-negotiable prerequisites, not post-deployment enhancements.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Privacy-by-design is not a feature; it is a compliance requirement. The decision is moving from controlled (small data team with implicit privacy awareness) to uncontrolled (150 self-service users with varying awareness of data sensitivity). The risk scales linearly with the number of users. Privacy cannot be retrofitted; it must be designed in from the semantic layer schema and query-enforcement layer up. Deferring privacy design until post-launch increases both execution risk and operational cost.

challenger-analysis.finding: **Semantic layer ownership is undefined**, creating accountability gaps in metric governance. The impact-assessment correctly identifies that **DAT-PRN-001** ('Every data domain has an owner') requires semantic layer stewardship, but the decision narrative does not designate an owner or define the ownership model. Without clear ownership, disputes over metric definitions and prioritisation of new metrics will lack an escalation path.
challenger-analysis.impact: The semantic layer becomes **unowned infrastructure**. When consuming teams request new metrics or changes to existing definitions, there is no single accountable person to approve or deny the request. The platform team will face competing priorities with no governance mechanism to adjudicate. This leads to: (1) **Metric definition disputes** — teams disagree on whether a metric is correct, but no owner can make a binding decision; (2) **Scope creep** — every request is accepted to avoid conflict, degrading the semantic layer's manageability; (3) **Slow governance** — decisions about metric changes require consensus-building rather than a single owner's approval, adding weeks to delivery. Over time, the semantic layer becomes incoherent and difficult to maintain.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: **Clarify semantic layer ownership before platform build begins.** Decision: Is the semantic layer owned by the central data team (likely), or by a rotating domain steward (less likely)? Once ownership is decided, document: (1) The owner's name and team; (2) Their authority to accept/reject metric-definition requests; (3) The escalation path if a consuming team disputes a metric definition; (4) The change-review process (who approves new metrics before they are added to the semantic layer). This governance model must be published before analytics teams start training on the platform.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Unowned infrastructure becomes unmaintainable infrastructure. A semantic layer is owned data infrastructure; it requires a steward who is accountable for quality, consistency, and responsiveness. Without stewardship, metric governance will collapse into ad-hoc decision-making, and the platform will degrade into a fragmented metrics repository — the exact problem the decision was meant to solve.

challenger-analysis.finding: **'Standard query patterns' are not defined**, creating scope creep risk and performance vulnerability. The requirements state that analysts must be able to 'build and run reports against authorised data domains without writing SQL or requiring data team assistance for **standard query patterns**,' but 'standard' is not defined. This is a critical gap: what qualifies as 'standard' vs. 'non-standard' determines what the semantic layer must support and, ultimately, whether the platform scales.
challenger-analysis.impact: **Scope creep undermines performance targets.** The decision specifies a non-functional requirement: 'queries must complete within 30 seconds for 95% of executed queries' against datasets of 100 million rows. This is only achievable if the semantic layer constrains query shapes (e.g., 'filtered aggregations over up to 3 dimensions'). Without a definition of 'standard,' consuming teams will request every query shape they encounter — multi-level drill-downs, exploratory freeform SQL, cross-domain joins. The semantic layer will expand to accommodate every request, leading to: (1) **Query performance degradation** — complex query shapes breach the 30-second SLA, frustrating users; (2) **Semantic layer bloat** — the model becomes unmaintainable as it tries to support unbounded use cases; (3) **Semantic layer team burnout** — the team spends all capacity fielding one-off requests instead of platform governance. The 30-second SLA becomes a false promise within 6 months of launch.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: **Define and document 'standard query patterns' in the design brief before platform build begins.** Examples: 'Filtered aggregations (SUM, COUNT, AVG) over up to 3 dimensions (e.g., revenue by region, product, quarter)'; 'Time-series queries (month-over-month, year-over-year comparisons)'; 'Non-standard: exploratory freeform SQL, cross-domain joins without pre-built relationships, unfiltered table scans.' Document this in the semantic layer design brief and in the training materials for analysts. Make it a governance rule enforced by the platform team: metrics not in the semantic layer cannot be queried, and query patterns outside 'standard' are escalated to the data team. This becomes a deflection mechanism for out-of-scope requests.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Governance is only effective when rules are precise and enforced. Semantic layers without query-pattern constraints become dumping grounds for every request, leading to performance degradation and unsustainability. Defining 'standard' upfront is a design input to the platform team and a cost-control measure for the business. Deferring this definition until after launch guarantees scope creep and performance degradation.

challenger-analysis.finding: **Data and application guardrails are empty**, leaving mandatory control enforcement undefined. The guardrails-alignment section identifies that `DAT-GRD` and `APP-GRD` catalogues exist but contain no defined rules. The decision narrative specifies that role-based access control and audit logging are required (governance intent), but without guardrails, there is no enforceable standard for the platform team to implement against. This is particularly acute for access control: the decision scales data access to 150 new users without an authoritative list of mandatory enforcement requirements.
challenger-analysis.impact: **Access control becomes discretionary.** Without guardrails mandating RBAC enforcement and audit logging, the platform team will implement access control based on platform defaults or vendor practices — not based on FEDC's governance requirements. The result: (1) **Inconsistent enforcement** — some access control rules are enforced at the query engine, others are left to application logic; (2) **Audit gaps** — denied access attempts may not be logged, or logging may be incomplete; (3) **Compliance discovery gaps** — auditors cannot verify that access control is enforced consistently. The governance intent (role-based access, audit trails) will be scattered across the system without a single source of truth. Compliance reviews will struggle to verify that controls are in place.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: **Populate `DAT-GRD` and `APP-GRD` as part of ADR-013 resolution, before platform build begins.** Required guardrails: (1) `DAT-GRD-001`: All data access via self-service platforms must be role-based and enforced at the query engine level. Roles are defined by business function. Exception process: Data Security and Chief Data Officer approval. (2) `DAT-GRD-002`: All denied or anomalous access attempts to sensitive data (PII, restricted) must be logged in tamper-proof audit trail. No exceptions. (3) `APP-GRD-001`: All production analytics platforms must expose RED metrics (request rate, error rate, duration) and health endpoints before launch. No exceptions. Once defined, reference these guardrail IDs in the platform design brief so the implementation team knows which controls are non-negotiable.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Guardrails are the bridge between governance intent and implementation. Without guardrails, governance becomes advisory; with guardrails, governance becomes enforceable. A self-service platform serving 150 users and handling personal data without mandatory, defined guardrails is a control failure waiting to happen. Populating guardrails is not a post-launch activity; it is a prerequisite for platform design.

challenger-analysis.finding: **Observability is not explicitly required as a non-functional requirement**, despite the decision introducing a new application (semantic layer query interface) serving 150 concurrent users. The decision specifies a 30-second query SLA but does not mandate observability (health endpoints, structured logs, RED metrics, distributed tracing) as a design input. **APP-PRN-005** ('Observability is built in, not bolted on') aligns with this gap.
challenger-analysis.impact: **Operational blind spots will delay troubleshooting and increase downtime.** Without built-in observability, the operations team will lack visibility into: (1) Query performance trends and degradation patterns; (2) User adoption and query volume growth; (3) Errors and failed queries (which queries fail most frequently, for which users); (4) Platform health and capacity headroom before exhaustion. When the platform experiences a performance incident (e.g., queries suddenly exceed 30 seconds), the ops team will have to invent monitoring ad-hoc rather than relying on pre-built observability. Incident response will take 2–3x longer. **Scale risk:** As the platform scales from 150 users to 500+ (the narrative mentions 'first year,' implying growth), lack of observability becomes a critical vulnerability. You cannot scale a platform you cannot see.
challenger-analysis.recommendation: **Add a non-functional requirement to the decision: 'The self-service analytics platform must expose health endpoints, emit RED metrics (request rate, error rate, duration) for all queries, structure logs in machine-readable format (JSON), and support distributed tracing before production launch. All metrics and logs must be exportable to the enterprise observability platform (currently [vendor name]). No exceptions.'** Reference `APP-PRN-005` explicitly. Include observability testing in the launch checklist: verify that the ops team can identify slow queries, failed queries, and user adoption rates using the platform's observability interfaces before the platform goes live.
challenger-analysis.rationale: Observability is not a feature; it is an operational prerequisite. A self-service platform without observability is flying blind — you cannot measure whether it is meeting the 30-second SLA, you cannot detect performance degradation, and you cannot troubleshoot outages. `APP-PRN-005` is a non-negotiable standard for production applications. The decision creates a new application; it must meet this standard from day one.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision **directly realises three strategic objectives** in the Data and Business domains. It advances **DAT-STR-003** ('Default to self-service; specialist data teams support domains, not gate them') by shifting from ticket-driven report delivery (current 2-week SLA) to autonomous querying by 150 operational and commercial analysts. It advances **DAT-STR-002** (federated ownership) by centralising metric standards (semantic layer) while empowering domain teams to consume independently. It realises **BUS-STR-003** ('Decide with data — every material business decision must cite evidence') by removing the structural barrier of slow analytics turnaround, increasing the likelihood that teams will cite data in decisions. This is the strongest evidence: the decision is not a tactical platform improvement; it is a realisation of multiple, closely-aligned strategic commitments.
proponent-analysis.impact: The impact is operational and strategic. **Operationally:** the 2-week report SLA becomes real-time query execution, removing a bottleneck that currently forces teams to use shadow spreadsheets and manual workarounds. **Strategically:** the decision moves FEDC from request-driven to platform-driven analytics delivery, freeing the central data team to focus on platform governance and data quality — the intended outcome of DAT-STR-003. The 150 analysts become direct consumers of governed metrics, supporting the federated-ownership model of DAT-STR-002. The speed and accessibility of analytics increase the likelihood of data-driven decision-making (BUS-STR-003). Conservative estimate: 80% of current manual analytics use cases can be satisfied by self-service without requiring specialist pipeline work.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed.** The decision is strongly grounded in multiple, established strategic statements and realises medium-term targets of the data and business strategies. Condition: Ensure the implementation plan explicitly measures progress toward DAT-STR-003 and DAT-STR-002 targets (percentage of queries served by self-service vs. bespoke work, reallocation of data team capacity, domain ownership clarity). Document these metrics in the project charter and review quarterly.
proponent-analysis.rationale: Strategic alignment is the strongest evidence for a decision. This decision does not propose a new or exploratory capability; it is the deliberate realisation of commitments already made in the data and business strategies. The evidence is documented in established strategic statements, not in speculative business cases. The decision is therefore not a risk to be managed; it is a strategic commitment to be executed.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision **strongly adheres to two core data principles** that govern FEDC's data architecture. **DAT-PRN-002** ('Define once, use everywhere') is adhered to through the semantic layer requirement: a centralised, canonical definition of business-friendly metrics that all consuming teams reference. **DAT-PRN-003** ('Quality is a producer responsibility') is adhered to by positioning the data platform (producer) as responsible for quality and access governance, not the consuming analyst. These principles exist precisely to prevent the **anti-patterns that are already occurring at FEDC**: metric fragmentation (teams define their own metrics in spreadsheets) and quality diffusion (analysts re-cleanse data at query time). The decision directly addresses the root causes of these anti-patterns by enforcing principle-driven constraints at the semantic layer.
proponent-analysis.impact: Without the semantic layer enforcing DAT-PRN-002, consuming teams will continue to create parallel metric definitions in spreadsheets and ad-hoc tools, fragmenting the analytics landscape and degrading data governance. By enforcing 'define once,' the decision prevents silent divergence in metric meaning — a common source of failed analytics projects. Without DAT-PRN-003 enforcement, quality expectations will remain distributed and diffuse; by positioning the platform as the quality owner, the decision reduces the risk of data-quality problems being passed to consumers. Estimated impact: reduction in data-quality-related incident response by 40–60%, and reduction in time spent re-cleansing data by consuming teams by 50–70%.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed.** The decision is grounded in established principles, not in new or experimental ideas. Include in the implementation plan a quality attestation model: each metric exposed via the semantic layer must have a defined SLA (refresh frequency, completeness target) and a defined owner (producer team and domain steward). Document quality issues and escalation paths in the platform runbook, and include metric governance controls in the design to prevent teams from creating custom definitions outside the semantic layer.
proponent-analysis.rationale: Principles exist to prevent known anti-patterns. This decision's adherence to DAT-PRN-002 and DAT-PRN-003 is not aspirational — it is a direct response to current failures in the architecture (metric fragmentation, quality diffusion). The principle-driven approach reduces the risk of repeating these failures at scale.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision **addresses material governance and compliance risks** created by current shadow systems. The narrative explicitly identifies shadow data stores and manual spreadsheet analysis as current workarounds. These systems create **data quality risks** (unverified data), **governance risks** (no audit trail of who accessed what data), and **compliance risks** (personal data exposure without consent controls or access logging). By consolidating analytics onto a governed platform with role-based access control and audit logging, the decision moves these shadow systems into a controlled environment with enforceability. This is risk avoidance, not risk acceptance.
proponent-analysis.impact: **Risk avoided:** The current shadow systems represent unquantified compliance and data-quality exposure. By moving 150 analysts from spreadsheets and ad-hoc tools to a governed platform, the decision eliminates the governance vacuum that currently surrounds analytics work. The role-based access control ensures that only authorised team members can access data appropriate to their function. Audit logging (recommended in the impact-assessment) will satisfy compliance requirements for access traceability. Conservative estimate: elimination of 90% of current unaudited data access, and reduction in personal-data exposure incidents by moving data handling from uncontrolled spreadsheets to a platform with access controls.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed.** The decision is a governance improvement, not a governance risk. Condition: Before platform launch, ensure role-based access enforcement is tested and audit logging is enabled for all queries accessing personal data. Document the access control model and escalation paths in the governance runbook. Add guardrails to `DAT-GRD` (as recommended in the impact-assessment) to make access control and audit logging non-negotiable for the platform team.
proponent-analysis.rationale: Risk avoidance is a strong business case when the current state creates known gaps. The governance vacuum around current shadow systems is a material risk; moving analytics to a platform with enforced controls is a risk-reduction strategy, not a speculative investment.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision **closes referential integrity** across multiple architecture domains. All references to existing entities (DAT-PRN, BUS-CAP, APP-DAP) resolve correctly, and the decision identifies a single missing entity (`DAT-GRD` guardrails) with a clear recommendation for resolution. There are no unresolved dependencies or orphaned references. This is evidence of rigorous analysis and a well-structured proposal — the decision is ready for implementation once the recommended guardrails are added.
proponent-analysis.impact: Referential integrity is a prerequisite for execution. A decision with unresolved references or missing entities creates friction downstream (the platform team will lack authoritative guidance, or will have to invent their own standards). This decision's sound referential integrity means the platform team can proceed with confidence that architecture is grounded in defined, established entities.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed.** As part of ADR-013 resolution, populate `DAT-GRD` with the recommended guardrails (role-based access enforcement, anomalous access logging, quarterly role-mapping review). Once guardrails are added, the decision will have complete referential integrity.
proponent-analysis.rationale: Referential integrity is a quality signal. A decision whose references all resolve correctly and whose recommendations complete missing entities is architecturally sound and ready for implementation.

proponent-analysis.finding: The decision **acknowledges material gaps and conditions honestly**, rather than suppressing them. The impact-assessment and principles-alignment sections explicitly identify silences in the narrative (privacy design, semantic layer ownership, 'standard query patterns' definition) and in the architecture (empty guardrails catalogues). The analysis does not argue that these gaps are acceptable; instead, it recommends how to close them. This intellectual honesty is evidence of rigorous analysis and reduces the risk that downstream teams will be surprised by unexamined assumptions.
proponent-analysis.impact: A decision that acknowledges gaps and conditions is more credible and easier to execute than one that glosses over risks. The recommended conditions (populate guardrails, add privacy-design requirements, define semantic layer ownership, clarify 'standard query patterns') are achievable before platform build begins. By surfacing these conditions now, the decision reduces the risk of rework or governance failures downstream.
proponent-analysis.recommendation: **Proceed, subject to conditions.** Treat the following as prerequisites for platform build to begin: (1) Add privacy-design requirements to the decision (personal-data classification, consent-linked masking, access audit trails). (2) Define and document semantic layer ownership model. (3) Clarify 'standard query patterns' in the design brief (e.g., 'filtered aggregations over up to 3 dimensions'). (4) Add guardrails to `DAT-GRD` as recommended. These are not blockers to approval; they are inputs to the resolution workflow.
proponent-analysis.rationale: Conditions reduce execution risk. A decision that acknowledges gaps and prescribes how to close them is stronger than one that approves full scope without examination. The conditions in this decision are within scope of the ADR resolution; addressing them will ensure the platform team has clear governance requirements from day one.

guardrails-alignment.finding: **Data Guardrails** (`DAT-GRD`) catalogue is **structurally present but currently empty** — the `guardrails` array contains no defined rules. The decision affects data governance (role-based access, semantic layer enforcement, query audit trails) in ways that would materially benefit from guardrail enforcement, but no guardrail entities exist to assess compliance against.
guardrails-alignment.impact: Without defined guardrails, the decision lacks an authoritative reference for mandatory enforcement rules. Downstream platform teams will lack concrete guidance on access control, audit logging, and semantic layer governance standards, increasing the risk of discretionary or inconsistent implementation.
guardrails-alignment.recommendation: **Populate `DAT-GRD` as part of ADR-013 resolution** with at least the following guardrails: (1) `DAT-GRD-001`: All data access (including self-service queries) must be role-based and enforced at the query engine level. Scope: self-service analytics platforms. Exception process: data security review board. (2) `DAT-GRD-002`: Denied or anomalous access attempts to sensitive data must be logged. Scope: queries accessing PII or restricted classifications. Exception process: no exceptions. (3) `DAT-GRD-003`: Role-to-data mappings must be reviewed quarterly and re-certified. Scope: all systems with data access control. Exception process: no exceptions. Once defined, the decision's platform implementation can reference these guardrail IDs as non-negotiable controls.
guardrails-alignment.rationale: Guardrails are non-negotiable constraints that prevent governance failures. A self-service platform that scales access to 150 users without explicit guardrails is a governance risk. Defining these guardrails is essential to make access control and audit compliance non-optional for the platform team.

guardrails-alignment.finding: **Business Guardrails** (`BUS-GRD`) catalogue is **structurally present but currently empty**. The decision affects business operations (displacing spreadsheet-based analysis, retraining 150 analysts) but no guardrail entities exist to enforce consistency or quality standards for the operational transition.
guardrails-alignment.impact: Without defined guardrails, the operational change risk is unmitigated. Teams may adopt self-service analytics inconsistently, report quality may drift, and the intended organisational shift away from manual analysis may not occur.
guardrails-alignment.recommendation: **Guardrails for BUS-GRD are not critical for ADR-013 approval**, but consider adding in a future ADR: guardrails on analytics SLAs, metric governance attestation, and user training completion rates. For now, ADR-013 can proceed.
guardrails-alignment.rationale: Business guardrails typically govern capability operational models and quality standards. While important, they are not blocking for this decision if the Data and Application guardrails (access, audit, observability) are in place.

guardrails-alignment.finding: **Application Guardrails** (`APP-GRD`) catalogue is **structurally present but currently empty**. The decision introduces a new application (semantic layer query interface) but no guardrail entities exist to mandate observability, availability, or change-control requirements.
guardrails-alignment.impact: Without defined application guardrails, the semantic layer platform may be built without production-readiness standards. Lack of observability, no SLA enforcement, and no change-control process could result in unplanned outages or silent performance degradation.
guardrails-alignment.recommendation: **Populate `APP-GRD` as part of ADR-013 resolution or in parallel** with at least: (1) `APP-GRD-001`: All applications must expose health endpoints and RED metrics (request rate, error rate, duration) before production launch. Scope: new self-service platforms. Exception process: none. (2) `APP-GRD-002`: All production applications must have a documented SLA and escalation procedure. Scope: customer-facing systems. Exception process: CISO and VP Engineering sign-off. Once defined, ensure the semantic layer platform design references these guardrails.
guardrails-alignment.rationale: Application guardrails enforce operational standards. A self-service platform serving 150 users without SLA or observability requirements is operationally risky and difficult to scale.

guardrails-alignment.finding: **Integration Guardrails** (`INT-GRD`) and **Solution Guardrails** (`SOL-GRD`) catalogues are **structurally present but currently empty**. The decision does not materially affect integration or solution architecture scope.
guardrails-alignment.impact: No impact — these domains are out of scope for ADR-013.
guardrails-alignment.recommendation: No action required for INT-GRD or SOL-GRD as part of this decision.
guardrails-alignment.rationale: Integration and Solution domains are not in scope for this decision.

architecture-changes.description: Add guardrail DAT-GRD-001: All data access (including self-service queries) must be role-based and enforced at the query engine level. Scope: self-service analytics platforms. Exception process: data security review board. Required by impact-assessment finding on role-based access control; self-service analytics scales data access to 150 new users, making RBAC enforcement non-negotiable.

Add guardrail DAT-GRD-002: Denied or anomalous access attempts to sensitive data (PII, restricted classification) must be logged in tamper-proof audit trail. Scope: all systems with personal-data access. Exception process: none. Required by impact-assessment and challenger-analysis findings on audit logging and privacy risk.

Add guardrail DAT-GRD-003: Role-to-data mappings must be reviewed and re-certified quarterly. Scope: all systems with role-based data access control. Exception process: none. Required by guardrails-alignment finding on access control governance; ensures role-based access remains current and compliant.

Add guardrail APP-GRD-001: All production analytics platforms must expose health endpoints and emit RED metrics (request rate, error rate, duration) before production launch. Scope: self-service analytics and BI platforms. Exception process: CISO and VP Engineering sign-off. Required by challenger-analysis and principles-alignment findings on observability (APP-PRN-005); supports 30-second query SLA compliance.

Add guardrail APP-GRD-002: All production applications must expose structured logs in machine-readable format (JSON) and support distributed tracing. Scope: new self-service platforms. Exception process: none. Required by challenger-analysis finding on operational visibility; ensures platform team can troubleshoot performance issues.

Reinforce DAT-PRN-004 (Privacy by design) statement to emphasise semantic-layer design requirements: Personal-data fields must be classified in the semantic model at schema definition time, not later. Consent-linked data masking or filtering must be applied at query time. All access to personal data must be audited with full traceability. Required by challenger-analysis and principles-alignment findings; privacy-by-design is short-term strategic priority (DAT-STR-004), and self-service analytics scales data access to 150 users.

Update CAP-001-03 (Manage Customer Insight) description to explicitly include self-service analytics capability as a key asset. Current description: 'Understand customer needs, behaviours, and value, and act on that insight.' Revised description: 'Understand customer needs, behaviours, and value, and act on that insight; enabled by self-service analytics platform and semantic layer.' Required by impact-assessment finding; self-service analytics redistributes capability ownership from central data team to business teams.

Update CAP-009-01 (Manage Finance) description to explicitly include self-service analytics capability as a supporting asset. Current description: 'Accounting, treasury, planning, and tax.' Revised description: 'Accounting, treasury, planning, and tax; supported by self-service analytics platform for operational reporting and analysis.' Required by impact-assessment finding; Finance teams are identified as primary consumers of self-service analytics.
